Treatment regimens recommend an initial intensive phase of 2 to 3 months that is aimed at achieving rapid spu- tum conversion followed by a continuation phase of 4 to 6 months to eliminate residual bacilli and prevent relapse. The choice of regimen depends on local patterns of drug resistance and the availability of drugs, and are embodied in national and regional treatment protocols in many coun- tries including those in Europe,3 the UK,4 and USA.5 WHO recommended treatment regimens6,7 are based on disease severity and history of previous tuberculosis treat- ment. • New cases of pulmonary or extrapulmonary tuberculo- sis are treated with an initial phase consisting of ri- fampicin (R), isoniazid (H), pyrazinamide (Z), and ethambutol (E) for 2 months, followed by a continuation phase with rifampicin and isoniazid for 4 months, such a regimen being described as: RHZE2/RH4. Rifampicin may be substituted with ethambutol in the continuation phase to reduce costs, although this regimen needs to be given for a total of 8 months and is associated with an increased risk of relapse (RHZE2/HE6). In tuberculous meningitis ethambutol should be replaced with strepto- mycin (S) (RHZS2) and a 6- to 10-month continuation phase with rifampicin and isoniazid is often recom- mended. Ethambutol may be omitted from the intensive phase in patients with less severe forms of extrapulmo- nary tuberculosis or with limited non-cavitary smear- negative pulmonary tuberculosis if drug resistance has been excluded or the risk of drug resistance is deemed to be low (RHZ2/RH4). Cure rates of greater than 90% are typically achieved in patients infected with drug-sus- ceptible organisms who adhere to therapy. • In patients previously treated for tuberculosis, the ini- tial treatment phase is rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazina- mide, and ethambutol given for 3 months with strepto- mycin being added for the first 2 months. The continuation phase includes 3 drugs (rifampicin, isoni- azid, and ethambutol) and is extended to 5 months (RHZES2/RHZE1/RHE5). Because it is relatively cheap thioacetazone has been used in some countries with limited resources but its use is strongly discour- aged because of its weak antimycobacterial activity and associated risk of fatal skin toxicity, particularly in HIV patients. All first-line drugs can be given intermittently (at double doses 3 times each week) as an alternative to daily use. Patients who remain smear-positive at the end of supervised short-course chemotherapy may have drug-resistant tuberculosis and treatment usually re- quires the introduction of second-line drugs (see below).
